title: The sudden temper: explosive disorder or something else?
objective: Diagnose intermittent explosive disorder only after ruling out the conditions that also cause episodic aggression.

bookRef.book: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th ed.

content.vignette: Arjun, 31, a bank cashier in Pune, comes after his fiance threatened to call off the wedding. Four or five times a year, over something small (a slow auto driver, a misplaced file), he shouts, punches walls and once smashed his phone. Each outburst lasts under half an hour and he is ashamed afterwards, apologising for days. Between episodes colleagues describe him as gentle and helpful. He drinks two beers on some weekends, never before outbursts. No head injury, no fits, no mood swings lasting days, no unusual beliefs. Physical examination and routine bloods are normal.
content.question: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
content.explanation: Discrete outbursts out of proportion to the trigger, quick spontaneous settling, real remorse and no aggression or impulsivity between episodes fit intermittent explosive disorder. It is a diagnosis of exclusion: there is no pervasive disregard for others (antisocial), no chronic instability of self-image and relationships with fear of abandonment (borderline), no link between drinking and episodes (intoxication), and no sustained mood episode (bipolar). The work-up should still include toxicology and a neurological history, because epilepsy, brain lesions and endocrine problems are on the exclusion list.

distractorNotes.1: Antisocial personality: lasting pattern of rule-breaking and lack of remorse; Arjun shows remorse and is kind between episodes.
distractorNotes.2: Borderline personality: anger sits within unstable relationships, identity and self-harm; none described.
distractorNotes.3: Intoxication: outbursts are unrelated to drinking.
distractorNotes.4: Mania: would need days of elevated or irritable mood with other symptoms.

reviewFlags: Confirm against current DSM-5-TR/ICD-11 criteria wording
Avoid portraying anger as a character flaw

title: Impulse or compulsion? Sort the behaviours
objective: Separate impulse-driven acts (sought for pleasure or relief) from compulsions (unwanted acts done to neutralise distress), while accepting that the boundary is blurred.

bookRef.book: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th ed.

items.text: A college student lifts cheap hair clips from a shop although she can afford them, feels a thrill, then hides them in a drawer.
items.why: The act itself brings gratification; the object is not needed. Classic kleptomania pattern.

items.text: A clerk re-checks the gas knob twenty times before leaving because he fears a fire; he hates doing it.
items.why: Unwanted, distress-reducing, linked to an obsessional fear: a compulsion.

items.text: A man feels mounting tension, starts a small fire in an empty plot and watches the fire brigade with excitement; he gains nothing else from it.
items.why: Tension then pleasure, no gain or revenge: impulsive (pyromania pattern).

items.text: A woman washes her hands until they crack after touching a doorknob, to stop thoughts of contamination.
items.why: Neutralises an obsession; experienced as senseless.

items.text: A young man plays an online game all night; he enjoys it at first but now feels driven to continue despite losing his job.
items.why: Begins as reward-seeking. The book notes such behaviours sit on the border and are best treated like addictive disorders; accept either answer with this explanation.

content.takeaway: Ask what the act is for: pleasure or relief of tension (impulse) or neutralising an unwanted thought (compulsion). Expect overlap.

reviewFlags: Gaming item deliberately ambiguous: UI should accept both bins and show the note

title: Night shift in casualty: the five questions
objective: Use a structured emergency approach: safety first, medical vs psychiatric, psychosis, risk to self or others, capacity for self-care.

bookRef.book: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th ed.

content.intro: It is 1 a.m. in a district hospital casualty. Police bring Ramesh, 58, a shopkeeper, who was shouting at neighbours that people were hiding in his ceiling. His wife says he was 'fine until yesterday'. He has diabetes. He is pacing, sweating and looks frightened.

nodes.text: Before you begin the interview, what do you do first?

choices.text: Check the room: exit route clear, no sharp objects, a staff member nearby, and approach him calmly and without threat.
choices.feedback: Safety of the patient and staff comes before history-taking.

choices.text: Take him into the small side room alone and close the door so he can speak privately.
choices.feedback: Privacy matters, but with a frightened, possibly paranoid man you should not block your exit or be alone.

choices.text: Ask the police to restrain him so you can examine him.
choices.feedback: Restraint is a last step after calmer measures fail, not a starting point.

nodes.text: A senior nurse suggests a different start. You make the space safe and introduce yourself calmly. Continue.
He answers some questions but keeps losing track and asks twice what day it is. Which features make you worry about a medical cause?

choices.text: Sudden onset since yesterday, first episode at 58, diabetes, sweating, and disorientation.
choices.feedback: Acute onset, first episode in later life, medical illness and impaired orientation all point towards a physical cause such as delirium or hypoglycaemia.

choices.text: The fact that he believes people are hiding in the ceiling.
choices.feedback: Persecutory content occurs in both medical and primary psychiatric states; on its own it does not separate them.

choices.text: Bedside glucose, vital signs, and a focused physical and neurological examination; ask about alcohol and recent medicine changes.
choices.feedback: Rule out the treatable and dangerous causes first.

choices.text: Give an antipsychotic injection and admit him to the psychiatry ward.
choices.feedback: Labelling him 'psychiatric' before excluding medical causes risks missing a life-threatening problem.

nodes.text: His glucose is very low. After treatment by the medical team he becomes calmer and oriented. Before deciding where he goes, which questions remain?

choices.text: Is he still psychotic? Any thoughts of harming himself or others? Can he look after himself at home tonight, and who is with him?
choices.feedback: These complete the five questions and guide disposition. Inform the treating physician and document clearly.

choices.text: None. The cause is found, so discharge him immediately.
choices.feedback: Even with a medical cause, you still check residual symptoms, risk and support before discharge.

nodes.text: Summary: safety, then medical vs psychiatric, then psychosis, risk to self and others, and self-care. Record findings, gaps in information and the plan.

reviewFlags: Clinical leads to confirm hypoglycaemia management wording is general and non-prescriptive
Restraint references should align with MHCA 2017 sections taught in ethics-law

title: Six weeks after the funeral
objective: Distinguish an expected grief reaction from a major depressive episode after a loss.

bookRef.book: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th ed.

vignettes.text: Lakshmi, 64, lost her husband six weeks ago. She cries when she sees his chair or hears his favourite bhajan, sleeps poorly, and eats less. She still cooks for her grandson, attends the temple, and laughs when relatives share stories about him. She says, 'I miss him terribly, but I know I must carry on.' She has no thoughts of being worthless and no wish to die.
vignettes.why: Sadness comes in waves triggered by reminders, self-esteem is intact, she can still feel pleasure, and functioning is only mildly affected.

vignettes.text: Prakash, 52, lost his father four months ago. He has stopped going to work, sits in a dark room most of the day, and moves and speaks slowly. He says he is 'a useless son and a burden to everyone' and that his family would be better off without him. Nothing cheers him, even when no one mentions his father.
vignettes.answer: Major depressive episode (needs full assessment, including suicide risk)
vignettes.why: Pervasive low mood independent of reminders, worthlessness, psychomotor slowing, passive death wishes and marked impairment go beyond grief.

options: Major depressive episode (needs full assessment, including suicide risk)
content.explanation: Features that point to depression rather than grief: morbid guilt or worthlessness, suicidal ideation, psychomotor retardation, mood that does not depend on reminders of the person who died, and lasting severe impairment. Grief and depression can coexist; when in doubt, assess fully and ask about suicide.
content.followUp: Prakash says he would be better off dead. What is your next step? (Answer: ask directly about intent, plan and means, and move to the safety-planning steps from the suicide module.)

reviewFlags: Suicide content: show helpline banner
Align terms with ICD-11 prolonged grief disorder taught in defences 3.5

title: Depression in the medically ill: swap the symptom
objective: Apply substitution criteria so that physical illness does not inflate or mask a diagnosis of depression.

bookRef.book: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th ed.

content.instructions: A patient with advanced cancer may lose appetite, sleep and energy because of the illness itself. Match each physical symptom to the psychological sign used in its place.

pairs.right: Not brightening when good things happen (lack of reactivity)

content.explanation: The book presents this substitution approach as performing as well as standard criteria. It reminds us that hopelessness and loss of reactivity are not 'normal for someone dying'; when present they suggest a treatable depression.
content.miniCase: Mrs Fernandes, 70, has metastatic breast cancer. She sleeps badly and has no appetite because of the disease. She no longer wants her grandchildren to visit, says 'what is the point', and nothing lifts her mood. Using the substitutions, is depression likely? (Yes: withdrawal, pessimism and lack of reactivity count where the physical symptoms cannot.)

reviewFlags: End-of-life theme: content warning
Check that pairing order matches the book table before publishing

title: Breaking bad news: the first two minutes
objective: Choose responses that prepare, check what the person wants to know, use plain language and promise continued care.

bookRef.book: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th ed.

content.setting: You are a psychology trainee in the oncology liaison team. The oncologist has told Mr Iqbal, 49, that his cancer has spread. Afterwards, sitting with you in a quiet room, he says:
content.clientStatement: They used a lot of words I didn't follow. Just tell me straight, how long do I have?

responses.text: Doctors usually say six months to a year for this stage.
responses.reason: Gives a survival estimate the book warns is usually inaccurate, outside your role, and without checking understanding.

responses.text: Don't think about that now. Stay positive and everything will be fine.
responses.reason: False reassurance closes the conversation and abandons his question.

responses.text: That's a very hard question, and I can hear you want honesty. Can you tell me what you understood from the doctor, and how much detail you'd like right now? I'll make sure you get clear answers from your oncologist, and I'll stay with you through this.
responses.reason: Acknowledges feeling, checks understanding and how much he wants to know, offers plain information through the right person, and promises non-abandonment.

responses.text: I am not a doctor, so I can't discuss that. You should ask the oncologist.
responses.reason: Correct about role, but abrupt; misses the chance to respond to his distress and to help him prepare his questions.

content.debrief: Good practice: private room, sitting at eye level, time set aside, simple language, information over more than one meeting, ask how much the person wants to know, never criticise their reaction, and say clearly that care will continue. In Indian settings families sometimes ask that the patient not be told; explore this with the family and the patient's own wishes rather than agreeing automatically.

reviewFlags: High sensitivity: terminal illness
Faculty to review family-collusion note against Indian consent norms

title: 'Help me end this': a request for hastened death
objective: Respond to a request for hastened death by assessing for treatable depression and unmet suffering, respecting autonomy within the law.

bookRef.book: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th ed.
bookRef.pages: file 2 PDF pp. 1118-1121 (global 2718-2721); depression in advanced disease p. 1090

content.vignette: Mr Dsouza, 74, has advanced motor neurone disease and is cared for at home in Goa by his daughter. During a palliative-care home visit he tells you, the counselling psychologist, 'I don't want to be a burden. Please ask the doctor to give me something to finish it.' He has been sleeping poorly, says he feels worthless, and stopped seeing his church friends a month ago. His pain is not well controlled.
content.question: What is the most appropriate first response?

options.text: Explain that his request is illegal and move on to other topics.
options.why: Shuts down a disclosure of suffering and possible suicidal thinking.

options.text: Take the request seriously, explore what makes life feel unbearable, assess for depression and suicide risk, and tell the team about uncontrolled pain and his isolation.
options.why: The book stresses that requests for death may be driven by depression, which is treatable, and by poorly controlled symptoms. Assessment and better palliation come first.

options.text: Agree that his wish is reasonable given his illness and help him discuss it with his daughter.
options.why: Accepts the request without assessing depression, pain or capacity.

options.text: Arrange immediate involuntary admission to a psychiatric ward.
options.why: Disproportionate as a first step; risk assessment should guide any change in care.

discussionPrompts: Separate withdrawing or withholding life-sustaining treatment from actively ending life. Which is permitted in India today, and under what safeguards? (Check current Supreme Court guidance and MHCA advance-directive provisions with faculty.)
How would you respond if his capacity is intact, depression is treated, and he still wishes to refuse a feeding tube?
What does 'not being a burden' mean in a joint-family context?

reviewFlags: High sensitivity: suicide and death; show helpline
Indian legal position on passive euthanasia and advance directives must be verified by faculty before release
Do not present any position as the 'right' moral view; answer key covers the clinical first step only

title: A threat in the counselling room
objective: Decide when confidentiality must give way to protecting an identifiable person, and what proportionate action looks like.

bookRef.book: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th ed.
bookRef.chapter: 28 Forensic and Legal Issues (Violent Patients; Tarasoff)

content.vignette: Vikram, 24, an engineering student in Hyderabad, has been seeing you for anger and low mood. Today he is tense and says his former partner's new boyfriend, Kiran, 'ruined my life'. He knows where Kiran stays, has been following him for a week, and says, 'This weekend I'll make sure he never walks again.' He refuses to discuss it further and says you must keep this secret.
content.question: What should you do?

options.text: Keep it confidential; breaking trust will end therapy and he may just be venting.
options.why: The threat is specific, has an identifiable victim, a time frame and preparatory behaviour (following).

options.text: Continue the risk assessment, consult your supervisor immediately, and take proportionate steps to protect Kiran (for example informing police and the person at risk, or arranging assessment for admission), sharing only what is necessary and documenting your reasoning.
options.why: Serious, imminent harm to an identifiable person activates the duty to protect; action should be clinically reasonable and limited to what is needed.

options.text: Post a warning in the college group chat so everyone stays safe.
options.why: Disproportionate disclosure to people with no need to know.

options.text: Tell him you will report him unless he apologises to Kiran.
options.why: Coercive bargaining is not a safety plan.

content.explanation: In the original US case a student's specific threat to a named woman was not acted upon and she was killed; courts later held that therapists must take reasonable steps to protect identifiable third parties. The book notes clinicians cannot predict violence accurately, so decisions rest on specific risk factors and careful documentation, not certainty. Apply the same reasoning under Indian professional codes and MHCA 2017.

reviewFlags: Indian legal basis for duty to protect is less codified than US law; faculty review of the explanation
Violence content

title: Crossing or violation?
objective: Distinguish benign boundary crossings from exploitative boundary violations.

bookRef.book: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th ed.

bins: Crossing - may be acceptable with thought and documentation

items.text: A client brings a box of homemade ladoos after the final session at Diwali; the therapist accepts one and thanks her.
items.why: Small, culturally normal token; no gain at the client's expense.

items.text: A therapist asks a client who runs a travel agency to book her family holiday at a discount.
items.why: Uses the relationship for the therapist's benefit: a dual relationship.

items.text: A therapist lends a client the bus fare home after her purse is stolen during the session.
items.why: A one-off practical help; should be discussed and documented.

items.text: A therapist talks at length about his own divorce because he finds it comforting to share.
items.why: Self-disclosure meets the therapist's needs, not the client's.

items.text: A therapist starts dating a client two months after ending therapy.
items.why: Sexual relationships with clients are unethical; the book notes the transference continues after therapy ends.

content.takeaway: A crossing becomes a violation when it gratifies the clinician at the client's expense. Protecting the boundary is always the clinician's responsibility.

reviewFlags: Check the dating item matches the RCI/professional code position taught in therapies 3.5

title: Brief psychodynamic therapies: who did what?
objective: Recognise the main brief psychodynamic models by their defining features.

bookRef.book: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th ed.

pairs.right: Brief focal therapy with a set end date, linking transference to parents
Exactly 12 sessions around one central issue
Short-term anxiety-provoking therapy with strict selection criteria
Broad focus, flexible technique, used even for long-standing obsessional and phobic problems
Crisis consultation service that shaped brief methods

content.followUpQuestion: Which client features do these models look for? (Answer: a clear, limited complaint; at least one meaningful early relationship; ability to engage emotionally and respond to a trial interpretation; psychological mindedness; motivation to change.)
content.explanation: The models differ in length and selection strictness but share a focus, an agreed ending and active use of the relationship with the therapist.

reviewFlags: Names are acceptable here but study.test.ts bans book names in module text; author names are fine

title: Put IPT in order
objective: Place interpersonal therapy tasks in the initial, middle or ending phase.

bookRef.book: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th ed.

items.text: Name the depression and explain how common and treatable it is
Agree on the main problem area, e.g. a role dispute with a mother-in-law
Link this week's mood dips to what happened in relationships
Practise handling painful feelings tied to the problem area
Talk openly about finishing therapy and the sadness it may bring
Review gains and list early warning signs for the future

content.explanation: IPT is time-limited and structured: diagnose and choose a focus, work on it, then end deliberately, treating the ending itself as a small loss to work through.

title: Staying curious: a mentalizing response
objective: Choose a response that invites the client to think about her own and others' states of mind instead of interpreting, arguing or reassuring.

bookRef.book: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th ed.

content.setting: Neha, 23, has a diagnosis of borderline personality disorder and has self-harmed in the past. She arrives agitated.
content.clientStatement: My best friend didn't reply for six hours. Obviously she hates me now. Everyone leaves eventually.

responses.text: You're projecting your fear of abandonment from your father onto her.
responses.reason: A deep interpretation when arousal is high; she is unlikely to be able to think about it and may feel blamed.

responses.text: I'm sure she doesn't hate you. She's probably just busy.
responses.reason: Reassurance replaces her mind with yours; it does not help her consider other possibilities herself.

responses.text: Six hours of silence sounds really painful. Help me understand: when you saw no reply, what went through your mind about what she might be thinking? Are there other things that could be happening for her?
responses.reason: Validates the feeling, then takes a curious, not-assuming stance that invites her to think about her friend's mind and her own reactions.

responses.text: Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself?
responses.reason: Risk must be checked given her history, but asked alone and first it skips the emotional moment; combine with an empathic, curious response.

content.debrief: MBT is collaborative: the therapist's curiosity about mental states (hers and the client's) is the tool. Under strong emotion, mentalizing fails, so slow down and ask rather than tell. Always keep risk in view.

reviewFlags: Self-harm theme
Ensure the 'partial' risk item is not read as discouraging risk assessment

title: Amma is forgetting things
objective: Separate depression-related cognitive difficulty from dementia and notice signs of elder abuse or neglect.

bookRef.book: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th ed.

content.intro: Saroja, 72, a retired teacher in Chennai, is brought by her son Mohan, who says she has become 'forgetful and useless' over three months since her husband died. She sits quietly with her eyes down.

nodes.text: During testing she often says 'I don't know' without trying, but when given cues she recalls most words. Her speech and naming are normal. What does this pattern suggest?

choices.text: Cognitive difficulty linked to depression is likely; assess mood fully.
choices.feedback: Poor effort, 'I don't know' answers, better cued recall and intact language fit depression-related cognitive dysfunction more than a neurodegenerative dementia.

choices.text: Clearly Alzheimer's disease; start a dementia medicine.
choices.feedback: Alzheimer's usually shows consistent global impairment, language problems and poor recall even with cues. Treat depression first and reassess cognition.

nodes.text: You ask to see Saroja alone for part of the interview. Mohan objects: 'She gets confused, I'll answer for her.' What do you do?

choices.text: Politely insist on a short private conversation, explaining this is routine for every patient.
choices.feedback: Seeing an older adult alone is standard and is when abuse or neglect may be disclosed.

choices.text: Let him stay; he knows her best.
choices.feedback: You may miss important information, including fear or mistreatment.

nodes.text: Alone, Saroja whispers that Mohan has taken her pension card and she is often left without meals. She has bruises on both upper arms. What next?

choices.text: Thank her, ask gently about safety, explain options, document carefully, inform your supervisor and follow local adult-protection and legal routes, while treating her depression.
choices.feedback: Financial exploitation and neglect are forms of elder abuse. Her safety and wishes guide the plan; involve the team.

choices.text: Confront Mohan immediately in the waiting area.
choices.feedback: Confrontation without a safety plan can increase risk for her at home.

nodes.text: Later a nurse notices bruises on Saroja's upper arms while checking her blood pressure. You arrange to see her alone. Continue.
Key learning: depression in older adults can look like dementia; always see the older person alone; abuse includes financial harm and neglect, not only hitting.

reviewFlags: High sensitivity: elder abuse
Faculty to add the correct Indian legal route (Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, local helplines) after verification

title: The new bride and the spirit
objective: Approach a possession presentation respectfully, separating dissociative possession from psychosis, epilepsy and deliberate feigning.

bookRef.book: Kaplan & Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th ed.
bookRef.chapter: 34 Contributions from the Behavioral and Social Sciences (Culture-Bound Syndromes: Possession Syndrome)

content.vignette: Kavita, 20, married four months ago and moved into her husband's joint family in a village near Varanasi. Her mother-in-law criticises her cooking daily. Twice in the past month, usually in the evening after an argument, she has fallen to the floor, shaken her head, and spoken in a deep voice saying she is a goddess who will punish the household. Each episode lasts about an hour. Afterwards she is exhausted and remembers little. Between episodes she is sad but has no hallucinations or unusual beliefs. She bit nothing, was not incontinent, and was never hurt in a fall.
content.question: Which is the most likely explanation?
options: Dissociative (possession) trance linked to family stress
content.explanation: Episodes are triggered by conflict, include an altered identity speaking in the third person with complaints about the family, and are followed by exhaustion and amnesia; she is well between episodes. This matches the South Asian possession pattern the book describes, often in young women facing stressful transitions such as moving into the in-laws' home. Psychosis is unlikely without symptoms between episodes. Epilepsy is less likely (situational trigger, long duration, no injury, tongue-biting or incontinence) but an EEG may still be considered if features are atypical. Malingering requires deliberate feigning for an external gain, which is not evident; labelling her a fraud would harm her and the therapeutic relationship.
content.nextSteps: Respect the family's explanation while exploring stress, mood and safety; work with the family on conflict; consider whether a traditional healer is already involved and how to collaborate safely.

reviewFlags: High sensitivity: religion, gender and family conflict - avoid stereotyping joint families or in-laws
Check alignment with ICD-11 possession trance disorder wording in more-disorders 4.2
